Series::softmax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::softmax(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

softmax() turns a lane of real-valued scores into a probability distribution over that lane: every output is in (0, 1) and the outputs along dim sum to 1.

softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j)

The dim argument chooses which axis is normalized. Every other axis is left alone, so on a [batch, classes] matrix softmax(1) produces one distribution per row.

Softmax is shift-invariant: adding the same constant to every score in a lane does not change the result, because the constant cancels between numerator and denominator. That property is what makes a numerically stable implementation possible (see the Numerical Stability section below) and it is why only score differences matter.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis to normalize over. Negative values count from the end. It must refer to a real axis; an out-of-range dim raises.

There is no whole-series overload — softmax is always taken along one named axis.

Returns¶

Series A distribution the same shape and dtype as the input. Values along dim sum to 1.

Numerical Stability¶

A direct exp(x_i) / sum exp(x_j) overflows to inf as soon as any score passes about 709 (for float64). softmax() uses the shift-invariance above: it subtracts the per-lane maximum before exponentiating,

softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i - m) / sum_j exp(x_j - m),   m = max_j x_j

so the largest exponent is always exp(0) = 1 and nothing overflows. The smallest terms may still underflow to 0 — that is correct behavior, and it is exactly where log_softmax() earns its place, because log(0) is -inf but log_softmax stays finite.

Gradient¶

softmax() is differentiable. Writing p = softmax(x) along dim, the Jacobian within a lane is

d p_i / d x_j = p_i (delta_ij - p_j)

so the backward for an upstream sensitivity g is

dx_i = p_i (g_i - sum_j p_j g_j)

— each input’s gradient is its probability times how much its own upstream signal exceeds the lane’s probability-weighted average. A consequence: softmax(x).sum(dim) is the constant 1, so its gradient is 0 everywhere.

Examples¶

Example 1. One distribution per row with dim = 1.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0},
    {1.0, 1.0, 1.0},
});

std::cout << scores.softmax(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.090030573, 0.24472847, 0.66524096],
  [0.33333333, 0.33333333, 0.33333333]]

Each row sums to 1. The second row is uniform because its scores are equal.

Example 2. Changing dim changes which lane is normalized.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0},
    {1.0, 1.0, 1.0},
});

std::cout << scores.softmax(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.5, 0.73105858, 0.88079708],
  [0.5, 0.26894142, 0.11920292]]

Now each column sums to 1.

Example 3. Negative dim counts from the end.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0, 3.0},
    {1.0, 1.0, 1.0},
});

std::cout << scores.softmax(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.090030573, 0.24472847, 0.66524096],
  [0.33333333, 0.33333333, 0.33333333]]

For a rank-2 input, -1 is the last axis, so this matches softmax(1).

Example 4. Large scores that would overflow a naive exp are handled.

auto big = pluss::make_series({710.0, 711.0, 712.0});

std::cout << big.softmax(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.090030573, 0.24472847, 0.66524096]

exp(710) alone overflows float64, but the max-shift keeps every exponent at or below exp(0). The result matches Example 1’s first row because the score differences are the same.

Example 5. The Jacobian in action: gradient of the first probability.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto p = x.softmax(1);
(p * pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0, 0.0}})).sum().reverse();

std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.081925069, -0.022033045, -0.059892025]]

With g = [1, 0, 0] the backward is p_i (g_i - sum_j p_j g_j) = p_i (g_i - p_0): p_0(1 - p_0) = 0.0819, -p_0 p_1 = -0.0220, -p_0 p_2 = -0.0599.

Example 6. softmax(x).sum(dim) is identically 1, so its gradient is zero.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.softmax(1).sum().reverse();

std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.5025235e-17, -4.0842823e-17, 5.5868057e-17]]

Zero up to floating-point rounding.

Example 7. An out-of-range dim is rejected.

try {
  pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}}).softmax(5);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • dim is required — there is no whole-series softmax. Pick the axis the distribution should live on.

  • Only score differences matter; a constant offset per lane is invisible.

  • The smallest probabilities can underflow to exactly 0. If you then take a log, use log_softmax(), which never produces -inf for a finite input.

  • For a classification loss, prefer log_softmax() directly over softmax().log() — it is both more stable and cheaper.

Summary¶

softmax(dim) normalizes one axis into a probability distribution:

  • exp(x_i) / sum exp(x_j), computed with a max-shift so nothing overflows

  • shift-invariant along the lane; only score differences matter

  • differentiable, Jacobian p_i (delta_ij - p_j)

  • pair with log_softmax() whenever a logarithm follows

See Also¶

  • Series::log_softmax: log(softmax(x)) without the -inf; the right choice for classification losses.

  • Series::logsumexp: the stable log sum exp that softmax’s denominator is built on.

  • Series::sigmoid: the two-outcome special case.

  • Series::amax: the per-lane maximum used for the shift.
